Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Renewable energy sources play an increasingly important role in the global energy mix, as the effort to reduce the environmental impact of energy production increases.

Out of all the renewable energy alternatives, wind energy is one of the most developed technologies worldwide. The U.S Department of Energy has put together a guide to achieving operational efficiency using predictive maintenance practices.

Predictive maintenance uses sensor information and analysis methods to measure and predict degradation and future component capability. The idea behind predictive maintenance is that failure patterns are predictable and if component failure can be predicted accurately and the component is replaced before it fails, the costs of operation and maintenance will be much lower.

The sensors fitted across different machines involved in the process of energy generation collect data related to various environmental factors (temperature, humidity, wind speed, etc.) and additional features related to various parts of the wind turbine (gearbox, tower, blades, break, etc.).

Objective¶

“ReneWind” is a company working on improving the machinery/processes involved in the production of wind energy using machine learning and has collected data of generator failure of wind turbines using sensors. They have shared a ciphered version of the data, as the data collected through sensors is confidential (the type of data collected varies with companies). Data has 40 predictors, 20000 observations in the training set and 5000 in the test set.

The objective is to build various classification models, tune them, and find the best one that will help identify failures so that the generators could be repaired before failing/breaking to reduce the overall maintenance cost. The nature of predictions made by the classification model will translate as follows:

  • True positives (TP) are failures correctly predicted by the model. These will result in repairing costs.
  • False negatives (FN) are real failures where there is no detection by the model. These will result in replacement costs.
  • False positives (FP) are detections where there is no failure. These will result in inspection costs.

It is given that the cost of repairing a generator is much less than the cost of replacing it, and the cost of inspection is less than the cost of repair.

“1” in the target variables should be considered as “failure” and “0” represents “No failure”.

Data Description¶

The data provided is a transformed version of the original data which was collected using sensors.

  • Train.csv - To be used for training and tuning of models.
  • Test.csv - To be used only for testing the performance of the final best model.

Both the datasets consist of 40 predictor variables and 1 target variable.

  • Feature Spread and Outliers: Several features exhibit large ranges and potential outliers (e.g., min/max values exceeding ±15), suggesting the need for normalization or scaling.

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Univariate analysis¶

In [21]:
# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.


def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to the show density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data= data, x= feature, ax= ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram

Comment:¶

  • Wind Speed (Mean, Median, Std):

    • wind_speed_mean: Distribution is right-skewed with values ranging from ~0 to ~15. A few observations >12 are outliers.
    • wind_speed_median: Similar pattern as the mean. Boxplot shows >95% of values concentrated below 10.
    • wind_speed_std: Long right tail, with extreme values >5 flagged as outliers.

  • Generator Speed:

    • generator_speed_min: Mostly centered around 5,000–6,000, with outliers below 4,000.
    • generator_speed_max: Spread is broader (~6,000–7,500), with clear outliers >7,300. Skewed right.
    • generator_speed_mean: Nearly normal, but some values above 7,000 are rare.

  • Torque Features:

    • torque_mean: Centered around 3,000–4,000, but tails extend to >5,000, showing outliers.
    • torque_variance: Wide spread with extreme outliers >2e+06. Highly skewed.
    • torque_kurtosis: Most values are <10, but some outliers reach up to >100. Severe right-skew.

  • Power Output:

    • power_output: Main mass of data is between 100–1,500, with sharp right skew. Outliers exceed 2,000.
      • Failure (Target):
    • failure: Clearly binary with majority class = 0 (~97%) and minority class = 1 (~3%). Class imbalance is evident.

  • Other Features:

    • Several other statistical metrics like wind_speed_skewness, generator_speed_kurtosis, and torque_skewness show long tails, confirming high variability and outlier presence.

Bivariate Analysis¶

Correlation of Features with Failure Outcome

In [25]:
# Combine features and target from the full dataset for correlation analysis
corr_matrix = data.corr(numeric_only=True)

# Plot correlations with the target
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix[["Target"]].sort_values("Target", ascending=False), annot=True, cmap='coolwarm')
plt.title("Feature Correlation with Target (Failure)")
plt.show()

Comment:¶

  • The feature V15 shows the highest positive correlation with the target variable (failure) at 0.26, followed closely by V16 at 0.25, and V11 at 0.24. These features may contribute significantly to predicting failure events.
  • Other notable positive correlations include V8 (0.21), V4 (0.14), and V17 (0.11)—indicating moderate association with failure.
  • On the negative side, V18 exhibits the strongest inverse correlation with the target at –0.29, followed by V36 (–0.23), and V2 (–0.18). These features are inversely related to failure and may signal non-failure tendencies.
  • Additional negative correlations worth noting include V22 (–0.14), V5 (–0.13), and V35 (–0.10).
  • While neural networks do not require feature correlation for training, these values provide early indications of variable relevance and can guide feature engineering or interpretation efforts later.

Pairplot of Selected Features Colored by Class

  • V13 and V17: A weaker negative relationship is observed, but the classes appear more overlapping, indicating limited separation capacity between failure and non-failure classes.
  • V21 and V17: Displays a mild positive correlation, with slightly better separation of the target classes compared to V13-V17. Failures tend to concentrate around a different region.
  • Diagonal KDE plots: Distributions for features like V13 and V21 show differing density curves by target class—further supporting their relevance in classification tasks.
  • Overall, V13 and V21 show promising patterns for distinguishing failure, potentially useful in feature selection or importance analysis.

Correlation Check¶

In [28]:

    vmax=1,
    fmt=".2f",
    cmap="Spectral"

plt.show()

Comment:¶

Correlation Heatmap Insights for ReneWind Project:

  • Multicollinearity: Several features exhibit high pairwise correlations above 0.80—e.g., V15 with V13 (0.87) and V26 with V23 (0.83)—suggesting redundancy. This can negatively impact gradient updates in neural networks by introducing noise or unstable weights. Consider applying dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA) or dropping redundant features.

  • Low Redundancy Across Most Variables: Most features show low-to-moderate correlations (between -0.5 and 0.5), implying they provide independent signals—beneficial for diverse representation in deep learning.

  • Symmetry Confirmed: The matrix is symmetric and diagonal values are all 1.0, indicating accurate computation.

  • Actionable Recommendation: Retain diverse features for model richness but reduce or combine those highly correlated to mitigate overfitting and enhance training stability.

Missing Value Imputation¶

  • There were few missing values in V1 and V2, we will impute them using the median.
  • And to avoid data leakage we will impute missing values after splitting train data into train and validation sets.
In [34]:
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
In [35]:
# Fit and transform the train data
X_train = pd.DataFrame(imputer.fit_transform(X_train), columns=X_train.columns)

# Transform the validation data
X_val = pd.DataFrame(imputer.transform(X_val), columns=X_train.columns)

# Transform the test data
X_test = pd.DataFrame(imputer.transform(X_test), columns=X_train.columns)
  • Missing Value Treatment:
    • A SimpleImputer with median strategy is applied, ensuring that missing numerical values are filled robustly—less sensitive to extreme outliers than the mean.
    • The imputer is fitted only on X_train, which avoids data leakage, and the same transformation is consistently applied to X_val and X_test.
    • All transformed datasets retain original feature names using columns=X_train.columns, preserving alignment across modeling stages.

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Write down the model evaluation criterion with rationale

In [38]:
def plot(history, name):
    """
    Function to plot loss/accuracy

    history: an object which stores the metrics and losses.
    name: can be one of Loss or Accuracy
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots() #Creating a subplot with figure and axes.
    plt.plot(history.history[name]) #Plotting the train accuracy or train loss
    plt.plot(history.history['val_'+name]) #Plotting the validation accuracy or validation loss

    plt.title('Model ' + name.capitalize()) #Defining the title of the plot.
    plt.ylabel(name.capitalize()) #Capitalizing the first letter.
    plt.xlabel('Epoch') #Defining the label for the x-axis.
    fig.legend(['Train', 'Validation'], loc="outside right upper") #Defining the legend, loc controls the position of the legend.

Comment:¶

  • Visualization Function (plot):

    • Plots training and validation trends for loss or accuracy.
    • Useful for detecting overfitting (e.g., rising validation loss while training loss drops) or underfitting (both losses remain high).
    • X-axis: Epochs, while Y-axis: Selected metric (Loss/Accuracy).
In [39]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5):
    """
    Evaluate binary classification model with emphasis on recall.

    Parameters:
    - model: trained model
    - predictors: input features
    - target: true binary labels
    - threshold: probability cutoff for positive class prediction

    Returns:
    - DataFrame with Recall, Precision, F1 Score, and Accuracy
    """

    # Get predictions using threshold
    prob_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    pred = (prob_pred > threshold).astype(int)

    # Compute metrics
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)            # Focus on class '1' by default
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)
    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)

    # Return metrics with recall first
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "Recall (Priority)": [recall],
        "Precision": [precision],
        "F1 Score": [f1],
        "Accuracy": [acc]
    })

Comment:¶

  • This Performance function returns four core metrics:

    • Recall (Priority) – prioritized due to high business cost of missing failures.
    • Precision – indicates inspection efficiency.
    • F1 Score – balance between recall and precision.
    • Accuracy – general performance, though less useful in imbalanced scenarios.

  • It works with probabilistic outputs from the neural network and uses a threshold (default 0.5) to convert to binary predictions.

Initial Model Building (Model 0)¶

  • Let's start with a neural network consisting of
    • just one hidden layer
    • activation function of ReLU
    • SGD as the optimizer
In [41]:
# defining the batch size and # epochs upfront as we'll be using the same values for all models
epochs = 50
batch_size = 32

Comment:¶

  • Epochs 50 ensures the model trains over 50 full passes through the training data — enough to capture learning patterns without overfitting early.
  • Batch 32 is commonly effective choice that balances training stability and speed. Small enough to generalize well and fast enough for computation.
  • Fixing these values up front standardizes model training for fair comparison across all neural network configurations in your ReneWind project.
In [42]:

  • This clears the current Keras session, resetting all layers and models previously created, freeing up memory and resources.
In [43]:
#Initializing the neural network
model_0 = Sequential()
model_0.add(Dense(128 ,activation="relu",input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))
model_0.add(Dense(1,activation="sigmoid"))

Comment:¶

  • A 2-layer neural network was initialized using the Sequential API.
  • The first layer is a Dense hidden layer with 128 neurons, using the ReLU activation function, and accepts 40 input features from X_train.
  • The second layer is the output layer, consisting of 1 neuron with a sigmoid activation function, suitable for binary classification.
  • This architecture is designed to predict the binary target variable Target, where 1 = failure and 0 = no failure.

  • Model_0 achieved a recall of approximately 85.5% on training data and 84.2% on validation data, indicating strong performance in detecting turbine failures (class 1) with minimal overfitting.
  • Loss steadily declined for both training and validation sets, with training loss reducing from around 0.12 to 0.04 and validation loss stabilizing near 0.06, suggesting a well-optimized model using SGD.
  • Recall improved sharply in the first 10 epochs, rising from ~47% to above 80%, then gradually plateaued—implying fast convergence and training stability over 50 epochs.

Here is the corrected analysis based on the attached output for Model_0:

Model_0 Performance Evaluation¶

  • Recall (Validation): Model_0 achieves a recall of 0.8468 on the validation set. This means it successfully identifies nearly 85% of actual turbine failures, which is crucial for minimizing false negatives and avoiding costly undetected breakdowns.

  • Recall (Train): The model delivers a training recall of 0.8694, showing that it effectively captures failure patterns with only a small generalization gap to the validation set. This indicates good learning without significant overfitting.

  • Precision: The validation precision is 0.9843, confirming that the model makes very few false failure predictions, thereby helping ReneWind avoid unnecessary inspections or maintenance.

  • F1 Score: A strong validation F1 score of 0.9104 reflects a well-balanced model that performs reliably across both sensitivity (recall) and specificity (precision)—key for operational trust.

  • Accuracy: The overall accuracy is ~99%, but given the likely class imbalance (few failure cases), this metric is secondary to recall for ReneWind’s business objectives.

✅ Business Insight¶

  • Model_0 delivers a high-recall, high-precision, and balanced classification profile, making it a robust baseline model. It aligns well with ReneWind’s operational goal of early and accurate turbine failure detection to reduce replacement and maintenance costs. This model can confidently serve as a benchmark for tuning or further enhancement efforts focused on boosting recall without sacrificing precision.

Primary Metric: Recall (especially for class 1 – failure detection)

Training Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.87 – Captures 87% of all actual failures, which is promising at baseline.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.99 – Very few false positives.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.93 – Strong overall balance between recall and precision.

Validation Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.85 – Slight drop, but still retains strong detection ability on unseen data.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.98 – False alarms remain minimal.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.91 – Stable and reliable classification quality.

✅ Business Insight (ReneWind Context):¶

  • Model_0 successfully identifies the majority of turbine failures with minimal false alarms, achieving 85–87% recall.
  • This level of recall supports proactive maintenance scheduling, reducing costly replacements by catching failures early.
  • Serves as a strong baseline, but further tuning may still improve recall closer to optimal levels.

Model Performance Improvement¶

Model 1¶

In this model, we incorporate an additional hidden layer and use the SGD optimizer with momentum to improve convergence stability and performance

tf.keras.backend.clear_session()

# Initialize the neural network
model_1 = Sequential()
model_1.add(Dense(128, activation="relu", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))  # First hidden layer
model_1.add(Dense(64, activation="relu"))                               # Second hidden layer (updated)
model_1.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))                             # Output layer

Comment:¶

  • I introduced two hidden layers with 128 and 64 neurons respectively in model_1, while Model_0 uses only one hidden layer with 128 neurons. This added depth in Model_1 enables it to capture more complex relationships in the data, which may lead to improved performance.

Comment:¶

  1. Consistent Loss Reduction: Both training and validation loss decrease smoothly over the 50 epochs, with no significant gap between them, indicating that Model_1 is not overfitting and is learning effectively.

  2. Strong Recall Growth: The recall improves sharply within the first 10 epochs and continues to rise steadily before plateauing just above 0.80, showing that Model_1 is becoming increasingly sensitive to detecting failures.

  3. Parallel Recall Curves: The training and validation recall curves are closely aligned throughout, which means Model_1 generalizes well to unseen data.

  4. Efficient Training: Since most of the performance gains in recall occur early, training could potentially be stopped around 20–25 epochs to save time without major performance loss.

0 1 [128] relu 50 32 sgd [0.001, -] xavier - 0.039651 0.060528 0.86937 0.84685 78.51
1 2 [128, 64] ['relu', 'relu'] 50 32 sgd with momentum [0.001, 0.4] xavier - 0.048759 0.062630 0.84459 0.81982 113.38

Comment:¶

Summary:

Model_1’s deeper architecture and momentum-enhanced optimizer did not outperform Model_0. Despite the structural upgrade, recall declined and both losses increased, suggesting this configuration was less effective.

  • Architectural Depth Did Not Improve Recall: Moving from 1 hidden layer to 2 ([128] → [128, 64]) resulted in a drop in validation recall from 0.84685 to 0.81982, showing that the added complexity did not translate to better failure detection.

  • Momentum Reduced Learning Effectiveness: Switching from plain SGD to SGD with momentum increased training loss (0.0396 → 0.0488) and did not close the train/val recall gap. This indicates momentum did not accelerate or stabilize learning in this setup.

  • Validation Loss Increased: Validation loss rose slightly (↑ from 0.0605 to 0.0623), implying weaker generalization than Model_0 despite added model depth.

  • Training Time Increased Without Benefit: Training time grew from 78.5s to 113.4s—a 44% increase—yet delivered lower recall and higher loss, making the extra cost unjustified.

Comment:¶

  • Recall on Training Data: The model achieved a recall of 0.8446, successfully detecting ~84% of failure cases during training. This supports early identification of issues and helps mitigate sudden generator breakdowns.

  • Recall on Validation Data: With a validation recall of 0.8198, Model_1 maintains reliable detection performance on unseen data, reinforcing its capability to support proactive failure prevention strategies.

  • Precision: The model achieved precision scores of 0.9843 on training and 0.9733 on validation. These high values indicate that most predicted failures were indeed actual failures—minimizing false alarms and unnecessary inspection costs.

  • F1 Score: A strong F1 score of 0.9091 (train) and 0.8900 (val) confirms a healthy balance between recall and precision, affirming the model’s effectiveness in prioritizing turbine maintenance without skewing toward false negatives or positives.

  • Accuracy: Model_1 sustained accuracy of 99.06% on training and 98.88% on validation—although less critical in an imbalanced scenario, these figures underscore the model’s robust classification power.

✅ Business Insight:

  • Model_1 is well-aligned with ReneWind’s operational goals. Its ~82% validation recall ensures the early detection of turbine failures, minimizing costly replacements and enabling optimized, cost-efficient maintenance scheduling.

Classification Report – Model_1¶

Primary Metric: Recall (Failure class = 1)

Training Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.84 – Slightly below baseline, misses more failures than Model_0.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.98 – Excellent; very few false alarms.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.91 – Balanced performance, though driven by high precision.

Validation Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.82 – Slight dip compared to training; lower than Model_0.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.98 – Maintains very high confidence in predicted failures.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.89 – Consistent, but slight performance drop from training.

✅ Business Insight (ReneWind Context):¶

  • Model_1 delivers strong precision but with a slight sacrifice in recall, detecting 82–84% of failures.
  • Though fewer false positives reduce inspection costs, it risks missing more actual failures, which could lead to costlier replacements.
  • Compared to Model_0, this is a slight trade-off, and unless precision is a higher priority than recall, Model_0 is the better fit for ReneWind’s failure minimization objective.

Model 2¶

To introduce regularization, we apply a 20% dropout immediately after the first hidden layer. This technique randomly deactivates half of the neurons during training, helping to reduce overfitting and improve generalization.

In [66]:
# Clear any previous model from memory
tf.keras.backend.clear_session()
In [67]:
model_2 = Sequential()
model_2.add(Dense(128, activation="relu", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))  # 1st hidden layer
model_2.add(Dropout(0.2))                                               # Regularization
model_2.add(Dense(64, activation="tanh"))                               # 2nd hidden layer
model_2.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))                             # Output layer

Comment:¶

  • Model_2 builds upon Model_1 by incorporating Dropout regularization (rate = 0.2) after the first hidden layer and switching the second hidden layer’s activation function from ReLU to tanh. These adjustments help reduce overfitting and improve generalization by introducing non-linearity and randomly deactivating neurons during training.

Comment:¶

1. Continuous Loss Decrease: Both training and validation loss decrease steadily over the epochs, with the validation loss consistently lower than the training loss, indicating effective learning without signs of overfitting.

2. Validation Recall Outperforms: The validation recall improves faster and reaches higher values (above 0.75) than the training recall (around 0.70), suggesting Model_2 generalizes better to unseen data than it fits the training data.

3. Smooth Learning Progression: The recall curve is smooth and steadily rising, especially for validation, indicating stable learning and convergence.

4. Slight Underfitting Possible: Since training recall lags behind validation recall, Model_2 might be slightly underfitting, and could benefit from additional capacity or longer training.

Here’s the corrected version based on the attached model comparison table:

📝 Comment:¶

Summary: Model_2 introduces dropout for regularization but suffers a noticeable drop in recall and an increase in both training and validation loss, suggesting that the dropout rate or network capacity may be limiting the model’s ability to learn minority class signals.

  • Regularization Trade-Off: Adding Dropout(0.2) led to higher training loss (0.0725 vs. 0.0488 in Model_1) and a drop in validation recall to 0.7613, down from 0.8188 in Model_1—indicating diminished sensitivity to turbine failures, likely due to underfitting or excessive regularization.

  • Lower Generalization Performance: Although Model_2 uses the same architecture as Model_1 ([128, 64]), its validation recall decreased from 0.8188 to 0.7613, reinforcing the need to carefully tune dropout strength when preserving recall is business-critical.

  • Training Stability Impacted: The training recall dropped to 0.7432, creating a smaller gap with validation recall (0.7613), implying more stable generalization—but at the cost of lower overall performance compared to Model_1.

  • Increased Training Time: Training time rose from 113.38s in Model_1 to 119.68s in Model_2. This is expected with dropout layers, which introduce noise into gradient updates and slow convergence.

Comment:¶

  • Recall on Training Data: The model captured ~74% of actual failures (recall = 0.7432), indicating that some failure events were still missed during training—leaving potential gaps in early failure detection.

  • Recall on Validation Data: Recall improved slightly on unseen data, reaching 0.7613, meaning the model misses ~24% of actual failures in production scenarios. This poses a moderate risk in terms of undetected breakdowns and associated replacement costs.

  • Precision: Very high precision of 0.9706 (train) and 0.9657 (val) shows that when the model predicts a failure, it's almost always correct—effectively minimizing unnecessary inspections or maintenance actions.

  • F1 Score: The F1 scores of 0.8418 (train) and 0.8514 (val) indicate a strong balance between recall and precision, with slightly better harmonic performance on validation than training—suggesting generalization is solid.

  • Accuracy: Overall accuracy is 98.5% on both train and validation sets. While this reflects consistency, it's less meaningful for turbine failure prediction due to class imbalance.

✅ Business Insight:

  • Model_2 achieves very high precision and improved recall on validation data compared to earlier versions, reducing both unnecessary costs and undetected failures. However, a ~24% miss rate (false negatives) may still be too risky for ReneWind’s operational reliability. A model with even higher recall, even at the expense of slightly more false alarms, may be better aligned with the business goal of avoiding costly generator replacements.

Summarized Classification Report – Model_2¶

Primary Metric: Recall (Failure class = 1)

Training Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.74 – Significantly lower than both Model_0 and Model_1, indicating more missed failure events.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.97 – Excellent at predicting only likely failures.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.84 – Decent, but suppressed by low recall.

Validation Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.70 – Further decline on unseen data, the lowest recall so far.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.98 – Maintains high accuracy in predicted failures.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.83 – Reflects the imbalance between high precision and low recall.

✅ Business Insight¶

  • Model_2 prioritizes precision over recall, detecting only 70–74% of failure cases.
  • This model will miss many at-risk turbines, leading to increased replacement costs and greater operational risk.
  • While efficient in avoiding false positives, it is unsuitable for ReneWind’s business objective, which emphasizes maximizing failure detection (recall) to minimize costly replacements.

Model 3¶

With the introduction of the Adam optimizer and a Dropout rate of 30%, we also apply class weights to address the class imbalance in our dataset. This combination helps the model focus more on the minority class while reducing overfitting, thereby improving its ability to detect rare failure events.

In [78]:
# Calculate class weights for imbalanced dataset
cw = (y_train.shape[0]) / np.bincount(y_train.astype(int)) # Convert y_train to integers

# Create a dictionary mapping class indices to their respective class weights
cw_dict = {}
for i in range(cw.shape[0]):
    cw_dict[i] = cw[i]

Comment:¶

1. Significant Overfitting Observed: The training loss is much higher than the validation loss, and the gap widens over epochs—a key sign of overfitting.

2. High Training Recall vs. Flattened Validation Recall: Training recall climbs steadily to around 0.923, but validation recall plateaus early near 0.89, indicating Model_3 is learning the training data well but not generalizing effectively.

3. Dropout Ineffectiveness: Despite applying a 0.3 dropout, the model still overfits, suggesting either inadequate regularization or model capacity exceeding data complexity.

4. Instability in Validation Recall: The validation recall shows random fluctuations instead of a stable upward trend—a possible sign of variance or learning instability.

Comment:¶

Summary: Model_3 is the top performer in terms of recall, confirming the effectiveness of handling class imbalance through class weights and applying moderate dropout, despite increased training time and loss.

  • Substantial Recall Boost: Validation recall surged to 0.8964, the highest among all models—up from 0.7613 in Model_2 and 0.8188 in Model_1—largely due to the use of class weights in training, which prioritized the minority failure class.

  • Dropout and Class Weights Synergy: Using Dropout(0.3) alongside class weighting helped balance underfitting risk and minority class sensitivity. The model generalizes well with strong recall and high training recall (0.9302), indicating it learned failure signals effectively without overfitting.

  • Slightly Higher Validation Loss: Validation loss rose to 0.0771, the highest among all models. However, the trade-off is justified given the substantial gain in recall—the primary performance metric for ReneWind’s failure prediction task.

  • Increased Training Time: Model_3 required 116.17s, longer than earlier models, due to increased backpropagation complexity from both dropout-induced noise and class-weighted loss computation.

Comment:¶

  • Recall (Train): With a strong recall of 0.9302, Model_3 captures over 93% of turbine failures in the training set, significantly reducing the risk of unplanned breakdowns in historical data.

  • Recall (Validation): The model maintains a solid recall of 0.8903 on unseen data, suggesting excellent generalization and reliability in identifying failures that require preventive repair.

  • Precision: At ~0.87–0.89, precision is slightly lower than in Model_2, meaning more inspections may be triggered, but this is an acceptable tradeoff given ReneWind’s preference to avoid costly generator replacements.

  • F1 Score: The model achieves F1 ≈ 0.91 (train) and 0.88 (val)—showing a well-balanced model with a recall-leaning tilt, suitable for high-risk failure environments.

  • Accuracy: While accuracy is ~98.7%, this metric is secondary due to class imbalance.

✅ Business Insight:

  • Model_3 offers the best recall performance so far on both train and validation sets, making it highly aligned with ReneWind’s goal of early detection. The slightly reduced precision is an acceptable cost compared to the significant reduction in missed failures, making this a strong candidate for deployment.

Summarized Classification Report – Model_3¶

Primary Metric: Recall (Failure class = 1)

Training Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.89 – Strong ability to detect true failure cases during training.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.99 – Very few false positives.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.94 – Balanced and impressive, indicating reliable training performance.

Validation Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.80 – A slight drop from training, but still solid generalization.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.98 – Maintains excellent prediction confidence.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.88 – Reflects a healthy trade-off between recall and precision.

✅ Business Insight¶

  • Model_3 effectively detects 80% of turbine failures, significantly outperforming Model_2 on recall.
  • With very few false alarms (high precision), the model strikes a solid balance, limiting unnecessary inspections while prioritizing high-cost failure prevention.
  • Given ReneWind’s recall-first strategy, Model_3 shows promising alignment with the objective to reduce costly unplanned replacements, while maintaining operational efficiency.

Model 4¶

To regularize the model, we apply 30% dropout after the first hidden layer to reduce overfitting. Let's observe its impact on the model performance.

# Initializing the neural network
model_4 = Sequential()
model_4.add(Dense(128, activation="relu", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))  # 1st hidden layer
model_4.add(Dropout(0.3))                                               # Dropout for regularization
model_4.add(Dense(64, activation="tanh"))                               # 2nd hidden layer
model_4.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))                             # Output layer

Comment:¶

  • Model_4 maintains the same structure and dropout rate as Model_3 (i.e., dropout of 0.3 after the first hidden layer) but uses a clearer annotation for “dropout for regularization”. It continues with the same hidden layer configuration and activation setup, implying no architectural change from Model_3.

Comment:¶

1. Slight Overfitting Present: Validation loss flattens early and remains higher than training loss throughout—suggesting some overfitting, though less severe than Model_3.

2. Stable and High Recall: Both training and validation recall converge near 0.90, showing strong and consistent learning on both sets.

3. Dropout Regularization Working Better: The use of dropout (0.3) is helping to control overfitting more effectively than in Model_3.

4. Model is Close to Optimal: Loss and recall curves suggest Model_4 is well-calibrated, with only minor room for improvement in validation performance.

Comment:¶

Summary:

Model_4 achieves the best balance between recall and validation loss so far, leveraging Adam optimizer with Dropout(0.3)—and without class weights—to outperform earlier models in generalization.

  • Strong Recall with Dropout Only: Even without class weighting, Model_4 reached a validation recall of 0.88739, only slightly below Model_3 (0.89640), proving that well-tuned dropout alone can effectively handle class imbalance to a large extent.

  • Best Validation Loss So Far: Validation loss dropped to 0.047665, the lowest across all models, signaling excellent generalization and strong confidence in predictions.

  • Efficient Learning with Adam: The Adam optimizer contributed to high recall (0.91779 train, 0.88739 val) and lower training loss (0.03011), even without class weighting—clearly outperforming all previous SGD-based configurations in both recall and loss.

  • Slightly Longer Runtime: Model_4’s training time was 116.38s, comparable to Model_3, due to Adam’s adaptive learning updates. However, the performance gain—especially in validation loss—makes this trade-off worthwhile.

Comment:¶

  • Recall (Train): Model_4 records a strong recall of 0.9178, indicating that over 91% of known failures are identified in the training set—critical for avoiding costly replacements.

  • Recall (Validation): With a recall of 0.8874 on unseen data, the model generalizes well, staying within a 3% drop from training—suggesting reliable early detection across turbines.

  • Precision: The model delivers exceptionally high precision at ~0.97–0.98, meaning that most of the flagged failures are indeed correct, minimizing unnecessary inspections and associated costs.

  • F1 Score: The F1 scores of 0.955 (train) and 0.929 (val) confirm a well-balanced model, leaning slightly more toward precision compared to Model_3, without sacrificing much recall.

  • Accuracy: Accuracy remains high at ~98.25–98.5%, although recall is the key business metric.

✅ Business Insight:

  • Model_4 strikes a near-optimal balance between high recall and very high precision, making it efficient and cost-effective. It is highly suitable for prioritizing true failures while keeping inspection overhead minimal, offering strong practical value to ReneWind's turbine maintenance strategy.

✅ Business Insight¶

  • Model_4 detects 89% of validation failures, a critical success in preventing costly turbine breakdowns.
  • Its perfect recall on training data suggests potential overfitting, but strong validation metrics support reliable performance.
  • For ReneWind, this model is a top candidate as it maximizes failure recall while keeping inspection efforts within practical limits, offering a cost-saving edge over less sensitive models.

# Initializing the neural network
model_5 = Sequential()
model_5.add(Dense(128, activation="relu", kernel_initializer="glorot_uniform", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))  # 1st hidden layer
model_5.add(BatchNormalization())  # Batch normalization after 1st layer
model_5.add(Dropout(0.3))          # Dropout after 1st hidden layer
model_5.add(Dense(64, activation="tanh", kernel_initializer="glorot_uniform"))  # 2nd hidden layer
model_5.add(BatchNormalization())  # Batch normalization after 2nd layer
model_5.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))  # Output layer

Comment:¶

  • Model_5 introduces both batch normalization layers after each hidden layer and retains dropout (0.3) after the first hidden layer, along with a glorot_uniform initializer. This model enhances regularization and training stability compared to Model_4, which had only dropout without normalization layers or custom initialization.

Comment:¶

1. Overfitting Noticeable: The validation loss begins increasing slightly after early epochs while training loss continues to decline—indicating overfitting despite the use of batch normalization and dropout.

2. Recall Gap Appears: Training recall climbs steadily above 0.92, but validation recall plateaus around 0.86, revealing generalization issues.

3. Batch Normalization + Dropout Combo May Be Too Aggressive: Despite being added to improve learning stability and generalization, the combo may be hindering validation performance.

4. Needs Adjustment: Model_5 is learning well on training data but is not transferring that learning effectively to unseen data. Possibly tune dropout rate or reduce batch normalization layers.

Comment:¶

Summary:

Model_5 delivers strong recall and excellent training stability, achieving the lowest training loss among all models. With its reliable generalization and efficient batch normalization setup, it stands out as a robust option—especially for mitigating overfitting risk.

  • Competitive Validation Recall: Model_5 attained a validation recall of 0.87838, just below Model_4 (0.88739) and close to Model_3 (0.89640). This confirms that batch normalization serves as an effective regularizer, even without dropout or class weighting.

  • Lowest Train Loss: It achieved the lowest training loss of 0.020202, indicating a strong and stable fit to the training data—largely attributable to the use of glorot_uniform weight initialization and batch normalization, which promotes efficient convergence.

  • Controlled Generalization Gap: The validation loss of 0.058822 is among the lowest across all models, suggesting the model generalizes well and maintains a good trade-off between training performance and validation robustness.

  • Slight Cost in Runtime: Model_5’s runtime was 119.22s, marginally higher than previous models—mainly due to the computational cost of batch normalization layers. Nonetheless, the performance benefit justifies the added time.

Helps stabilize learning by reducing internal covariate shift, which is amplified by multicollinearity.

Also accelerates convergence and may reduce the sensitivity to multicollinear inputs.

Comment:¶

  • Recall (Train): Model_5 achieves a very high recall of 0.9141, capturing over 91% of failure events in the training data—vital for proactive maintenance.

  • Recall (Validation): The validation recall holds firm at 0.8784, with only a ~3.6% drop from training. This suggests excellent generalization and stability in detecting failures on unseen turbines.

  • Precision: Precision is also extremely high at 0.9701 (val), reducing false alarms and keeping inspection costs low—a major financial win.

  • F1 Score: The F1 score of 0.921 (val) confirms a well-balanced model, slightly stronger than Model_4 on recall-precision harmony.

  • Accuracy: Model_5 clocks ~99% accuracy (train) and ~90.2% on validation, showing a slight dip in classification correctness—still acceptable given our priority on recall.

✅ Business Insight:

  • Model_5 delivers one of the best recall-precision trade-offs so far—high sensitivity to detect turbine failures while minimizing costly false positives. Its validation recall of 0.8784 and F1 score of 0.921 make it extremely well-suited for ReneWind’s failure prediction goal, especially under cost-sensitive conditions.

Training Data Performance:¶

  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.90 – Minimal false alarms for predicted failures.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.91 – Strong balance between precision and recall.

Validation Data Performance:¶

  • Recall (Failure = 1): 0.88 – Successfully detects 88% of real-world failure cases.
  • Precision (Failure = 1): 0.97 – Very few false positives, ensuring efficient maintenance targeting.
  • F1 Score (Failure = 1): 0.92 – High overall model harmony on critical class.

✅ Business Insight¶

  • Model_5 detects 88% of failures on unseen data, close to ideal for proactive turbine repair.
  • Compared to Model_4, it has slightly lower recall but significantly better precision (0.97) — meaning fewer unnecessary inspections.
  • This makes it an optimal cost-performance compromise, delivering high failure capture while containing inspection costs, aligning well with ReneWind’s goal of minimizing replacement and repair costs.

# Initialize the neural network
model_6 = Sequential()
model_6.add(Dense(128, activation="relu", kernel_initializer="he_uniform", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))  # 1st hidden layer
model_6.add(Dropout(0.5))  # Dropout for regularization
model_6.add(Dense(64, activation="tanh", kernel_initializer="glorot_uniform"))  # 2nd hidden layer
model_6.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))  # Output layer for binary classification

Comment:¶

  • Model_6 differs from earlier models by combining two weight initializers—He uniform for the first hidden layer and Glorot uniform for the second—alongside a stronger dropout rate of 0.5 for regularization. This design aims to enhance convergence while aggressively reducing overfitting compared to previous models.

Comment:¶

Summary:

Model_6 demonstrates the effectiveness of high dropout (0.5) in reducing overfitting while still achieving excellent recall. However, it comes at the cost of higher training loss, suggesting potential underfitting. It’s a viable option when generalization is prioritized, though dropout tuning could yield further improvements.

  • Excellent Recall Performance: Model_6 reached a validation recall of 0.89640, tying with Model_3 for the highest recall across all models—making it highly reliable for ReneWind’s failure prediction task, where recall is the top priority.

  • Trade-off in Training Stability: Despite leveraging both He and Xavier initializers with Dropout(0.5), Model_6 recorded the highest training loss (0.349311), indicating potential underfitting due to overly aggressive regularization.

  • Validation Loss Competitive: Validation loss was 0.079080, slightly higher than the best-performing models, but still acceptable—suggesting the model generalizes reasonably well even under strong dropout conditions.

  • Moderate Training Time: Model_6 completed training in 125.91s, the longest so far among all configurations. This is a trade-off for the heavy regularization, but justified given the recall-maximizing behavior.

Conclusion & Insight (Training Set)¶

  • Model_3 is the top performer on recall (0.9302), making it the strongest candidate for detecting turbine failures during training.
  • Model_4 (0.9178), Model_5 (0.9144), and Model_6 (0.9167) are close contenders, all maintaining a high recall while offering slightly better precision and F1 scores than Model_3—indicating improved balance.
  • Model_0, while having strong precision and accuracy, is outperformed on the priority metric (recall = 0.8694).
  • Model_2 remains the least viable, with a recall of only 0.7432, making it risky for failure detection use cases at ReneWind.
  • Final model selection should be based not only on training recall but also on whether these gains generalize well to validation data.

Summarized Insights:¶

High Recall:¶

  • Model_6 achieves a recall of ~87.6%, correctly identifying nearly 88 out of every 100 actual turbine failures. This minimizes missed failures (false negatives) and helps avoid expensive generator replacements—ReneWind’s highest cost risk.

Balanced Precision:¶

  • A precision of ~87.3% suggests that the majority of predicted failures are accurate, minimizing false alarms and controlling the cost of unnecessary inspections.

Strong Generalization:¶

  • The model maintains consistent performance across training, validation, and test sets, showing no overfitting and confirming its robustness on new turbine data.

Reliable Model for Deployment:¶

  • With a test accuracy of 98.6%, Model_6 demonstrates reliable, real-world applicability for automated failure prediction in ReneWind’s maintenance operations.

Conclusion:¶

  • Model_6 remains the strongest candidate post-deployment, offering the best trade-off between reducing costly false negatives and minimizing operational inefficiencies. It is well-suited for integration into ReneWind’s predictive maintenance pipeline.

Insights (Aligned to ReneWind’s Business Objectives):

Strong Recall on Failure Class (1) – 88%

  • The model correctly identifies 88% of actual turbine failures, effectively reducing false negatives. This is crucial for preventing unplanned breakdowns and avoiding costly generator replacements.

High Precision on Failure Class – 87%

  • With a precision of 0.87, only 13% of predicted failures are false alarms, meaning inspection resources are used efficiently—helping keep maintenance costs under control.

Near-perfect performance on Normal Class (0)

  • With 99% precision and recall for healthy turbines, the model almost never misclassifies them as failing. This preserves operational continuity and avoids unnecessary service interruptions.

Balanced Overall Performance

  • The model achieves macro and weighted F1 scores of 0.93 and 0.99, respectively—highlighting its ability to balance performance across both majority and minority classes, making it robust and dependable in real-world deployment.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

1. Deploy Deep Neural Network Model_6 for Failure Prediction¶

  • Insight: Model_6 delivered excellent test set performance with a Recall of 88.0%, Precision of 87.0%, and F1 Score of 87.0% (rounded from 0.8759, 0.8728, and 0.8743). On the validation set, it matched the highest recall (0.8964), tied with Model_3, and outperformed all other models in recall while maintaining better precision than Model_3.

  • Recommendation: Adopt Model_6 as the production model for automated turbine failure prediction. Its strong generalization ensures early detection of failures, preventing breakdowns and reducing emergency maintenance costs.

2. Emphasize Recall Optimization in Maintenance Strategy¶

  • Insight: Compared to baseline Model_0 (Validation Recall = 84.7%), Model_6 improves recall by +5.0 percentage points, ensuring more at-risk turbines are flagged earlier, saving potentially thousands in generator replacement costs.

  • Recommendation: Align predictive maintenance KPIs with Recall. Encourage detection of potential failures—even if it leads to a few extra inspections—because missing a failure (false negative) is costlier than investigating a healthy turbine.

3. Utilize Dropout and BatchNorm Regularization in Model Design¶

  • Insight: Model_6, which uses Dropout(0.5) with He + Xavier initialization, demonstrated superior generalization over under-regularized models like Model_1 and Model_2 (Recall < 82%). Also, Model_5 and Model_4, which used Dropout and/or BatchNorm, consistently outperformed simpler variants.

  • Recommendation: Use Dropout and/or Batch Normalization in future DNN designs to prevent overfitting and ensure consistent performance across evolving turbine conditions.

4. Prioritize Multi-Layer Architectures with ReLU–Tanh Activations¶

  • Insight: Two-layer architectures with [128, 64] neurons and mixed activations (relu, tanh)—as seen in Models 3 to 6—consistently outperformed single-layer setups like Model_0 (Recall = 84.7%) by learning more complex failure patterns. Model_6 reached 88% test recall using this structure.

  • Recommendation: Standardize multi-layer DNNs with diverse activation strategies as the preferred architecture for turbine failure models, ensuring better capture of nonlinear patterns linked to rare failures.

5. Integrate Real-Time Monitoring with Risk Thresholds¶

  • Insight: Model_6 achieved 98.6% test accuracy and confident recall performance, indicating its suitability for real-time predictions. This supports risk-tiered outputs for field action.

  • Recommendation: In deployment, apply risk-based alerting based on predicted probabilities:

    • High Risk (prob > 0.8): Immediate intervention
    • Moderate Risk (0.6–0.8): Schedule inspection
    • Low Risk (≤ 0.6): Monitor regularly

    This triage system ensures optimal use of inspection crews while maintaining safety.

6. Set Up Quarterly Retraining and Monitoring¶

  • Insight: Model_6’s training time of ~126 seconds (per runtime log) shows it’s efficient to retrain. Over time, seasonal patterns, mechanical wear, or environmental factors may shift turbine failure dynamics.

  • Recommendation: Establish a 3–4 month retraining cycle using updated turbine logs. Integrate live dashboards to track recall, precision, and class imbalance over time to ensure ongoing model reliability and responsiveness to data drift.
